claims.text: An HEA-specific interatomic potential can predict melting temperatures across a broad range of equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
The potential can predict enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The specialized potential is calibrated against first-principles data.
Classical molecular dynamics with a tailored potential is applicable to crystalline, near-equiatomic HEAs near melting.
The intended alloy domain contains five or more metallic elements, typically with each element at 5–35 at.%.
The specialized potential captures the relevant multi-element atomic interactions.
Embedding first-principles energy landscapes in the potential makes those interactions accessible to computationally efficient molecular dynamics.
The molecular-dynamics framework can model crystalline-phase disintegration and melting-related structural evolution.
The framework accurately models the enthalpic, entropic, and volumetric changes associated with melting.
Predicted melting temperatures and fusion properties will agree with experiments or first-principles benchmarks within approximately 5–10%.
The proposed simulations will require significantly less computational time than direct ab initio methods.
Experimental methods such as differential scanning calorimetry require extensive experimental runs to cover HEA composition space.
Generic interatomic potentials fail to capture the full thermodynamic picture across the HEA composition space.
The method is expected to be robust for near-equiatomic HEAs containing five or more elements.
Non-equiatomic or heavily phase-separated alloys may require refinement of the method.
The exact error margins and transferability across all HEA compositions and extreme conditions remain unvalidated.
Consistent deviations exceeding approximately 10%, or failure to reproduce qualitative phase-transition trends, would falsify the proposed accuracy claim.
